new_statements.relation_note: The catalog holds a record for this language with an EMPTY rule and no existing statements, so this is the first placement statement found: fixed final stress. The dictionary is explicitly pan-dialectal Guajajara-Tenetehar (introduction, p. 2: 'Fala-se uma única língua tupi-guarani, porém com cinco dialetos', Tembé being the most divergent), compiled from data begun in 1961 by David and Margaret Bendor-Samuel and continued by the Harrisons from 1970, mainly at Campo Alegre / Posto Zutíua (Araribóia area, Maranhão).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final syllable of nouns and verbs; a postposition is stressed (on its final syllable) only when it carries a prefix, which implies that bare postpositions are unstressed/clitic-like.
new_statements.exceptions: Postpositions: stressed only when prefixed (otherwise, by implication, unstressed). No other exceptions given; the statement is one sentence and gives no examples or stress marks in the entries (the orthography does not mark stress).
new_statements.identity_note: Harrison & Harrison 2013 describe Guajajara-Tenetehar as one language with five dialects (Corda/Mearim, Grajaú, Pindaré, Zutíua/Araribóia, and Tembé, the most divergent) and worked mainly at Campo Alegre / Posto Zutíua (Maranhão); the stress statement is given for the language as a whole. Eiró 2002 describes Tembé of the Gurupi river (c. 400 speakers, two age-graded varieties). Bendor-Samuel 1972 (unopened) is Guajajara of the Santa Inês area (Maranhão), where his 1961 fieldwork began.

new_statements.quote: [p.40, 5.0] In almost every case the final syllable of a nominal, verbal, adverbial, or down-ranked sentence phrase (cf. Chap. 8) is also the final syllable of a foot. The final syllable of a foot is heavily stressed, as described below, and heavy stress is thus often present on the final syllable of words (cf. Chap. 3.2, fn. 4). [p.42, 5.12] The final syllable of the foot, and it alone, is heavily stressed. If there are any other syllables, one of these is always medium stressed. More than one syllable may be medium stressed, but this is very rare and generally confined to feet having a large number of syllables. All remaining syllables are lightly stressed.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (da Silva 2010: stress on the last syllable) and as the Harrison & Harrison 2013 statement (final syllable of nouns and verbs; on postpositions when they occur with prefixes): Bendor-Samuel's rule that a relational phrase is stressed on the relatee's final syllable unless the relatee is a prefix is exactly Harrison's postposition clause. Adds: the stress domain is the foot/phrase rather than the morphological word, a three-degree system with semantically placed medium stress, isochronous feet, and the claim that heavy-stress position is not phonologically predictable at span level. It is silent on da Silva's penultimate-stress cases (case suffixes, negat…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Guajajara stress is described within a phonological 'foot' (one to five or more syllables, roughly coextensive with a grammatical phrase or word): the foot-final syllable, and only it, carries heavy stress; since nominal, verbal, adverbial and down-ranked sentence phrases almost always end at a foot boundary, heavy stress regularly falls on the final syllable of words. The final syllable of an auxiliary verb or of a relational phrase (postposition) is commonly NOT foot-final, the heavy stress falling instead on the final syllable of the relatee, unless the relatee is a prefix (pp. 40-41). Heavy stress is predictable within the foot but not within the span, because its position is what defines the foot division (p. 43); feet tend to isochrony (5.13). Sec. 5.3 considers and rejects an alternative analysis with foot-initial heavy stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Three degrees (heavy, medium, light): in any foot of two or more syllables one non-final syllable is medium-stressed (rarely more than one, in long feet); which non-final syllable is medium-stressed 'appears to be determined by semantic factors rather than to be the result of a predictable phonological pattern' (p. 42-43); all other syllables lightly stressed (short, indistinct, reduced; see 6.2).
new_statements.exceptions: Auxiliary verbs and relational phrases (postpositions) commonly do not end a foot, so their final syllable is not heavily stressed unless the relatee element is a prefix (p. 41); span-level tune, emphasis and hesitation modify foot length and overall stress degree (5.13, 5.16); when a high-rank grammatical unit spans several feet the non-final feet are slightly weakened and the unit-final foot slightly strengthened (5.16). No mention of the penultimate pattern with case suffixes / negative -i reported by da Silva 2010.
new_statements.identity_note: Bendor-Samuel 1972 describes Guajajara (the Maranhão variety of Tenetehára; SIL fieldwork, 1960s), not Tembé; the catalog record (da Silva 2010) covers both Tembé and Guajajára and the Harrison dictionary statement is Guajajára.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim in the extracted text we hold of da Silva 2010 at the stated lines/pages. (2) The deciding source is a 2010 historical-comparative PhD whose synchronic phonology section is brief and second-order (built on Eiró 2001), but it is a modern specialist work covering both dialects, and two independent sources downloaded now agree with the classification: Harrison & Harrison 2013 (SIL, decades of Guajajára fieldwork) state final stress on nouns/verbs, and Eiró 2002's Tembé transcriptions show final stress plus penult stress before negative -i exactly as coded. Carvalho 2001 and Castro 2017 (both downloaded, open) are silent on stress. tone.quote: Stressed syllables, marked in the phonetic transcription with an acute accent, are characterized by a combination of higher pitch, greater length and increased forcefulness as compared with unstressed syllables. Stress falls regularly on the last syllable of a word and is not indicated in the phonemic transcription. [mó] /mo/ 'yes' [tatá] /tata/ 'fire' [temi'ú] /temi'u/ 'food' ... [mukáw] /mukaw/ 'gun' [ma'eřo'okwéřə] /ma'ero'okwer/ 'flesh'
tone.locator: section 3 'Stress', p. 5; sections 1-2 'Chart/Description of Phonemes' pp. 2-5 list only consonants and vowels
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: No tone system posited: phoneme inventory = consonants and six vowels only; pitch (high) is one of three phonetic correlates of stress; stress fixed on the word-final syllable, predictable, hence unmarked phonemically. (Span-level pitch patterns/intonation are treated in the author's 1972 book, already listed here.).
